That file is loaded on top of whatever theme GTK4 is using, so you can override any style there without touching system files. If it doesn't exist yet, just create it.

**Key things to know:**

- Changes take effect when you restart the app (or log out/in for persistent effect)
- You can force a reload in some apps with `Ctrl+Shift+I` (GTK Inspector) if it's enabled
- GTK4's CSS is similar to web CSS but not identical — many standard properties work, but some web CSS features don't exist

**Quick example** to change a background color:

```css
window {
  background-color: #1e1e2e;
}
```

**To find what to target**, enable the GTK Inspector:

```bash
gsettings set org.gtk.Settings.Debug enable-inspector-keybinding true
```

Then open your app and press `Ctrl+Shift+D` to inspect elements and their CSS class names.

If you want system-wide theme overrides instead (affects all users), the path would be `/usr/share/themes/<ThemeName>/gtk-4.0/gtk.css`, but the user-level `~/.config/gtk-4.0/gtk.css` is the recommended approach.

H: how do I know what percent contrast ratio it is

A: 
Contrast ratio (X:1) doesn't directly convert to a percentage — it's its own scale. But here are two ways to think about it:

**As a fraction of maximum possible contrast:**
The highest achievable contrast is 21:1 (pure black on pure white).
14.3 / 21 = **68% of maximum**

**Simple brightness difference** (a rougher formula some tools use):
(226 − 19) / 255 = 207 / 255 = **81%**

Neither is an official WCAG measurement — WCAG only uses the X:1 ratio. The industry convention is:

| Ratio | Informal reading |
|---|---|
| 21:1 | Perfect (100% of max) |
| 14:1 | Excellent (~68% of max) |
| 7:1 | Good — AAA |
| 4.5:1 | Acceptable — AA |
| 3:1 | Marginal — AA (large text only) |
| < 3:1 | Failing |

Your 14.3:1 is objectively excellent contrast. The readability issue you're seeing is not the colors — it's almost certainly the **10pt monospace font** being too small at your DPI. Try bumping to 12pt.

H: how do i know when good or bad contrast. i just mean percentage as a simple way to find out

A: 
The simplest mental model — express the ratio as a percent of the maximum (21:1):

```
your_ratio / 21 × 100 = %
```

**Thresholds:**

| % of max | Ratio | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| > 33% | > 7:1 | Great — WCAG AAA |
| 21–33% | 4.5–7:1 | Okay — WCAG AA |
| 14–21% | 3–4.5:1 | Marginal — large text only |
| < 14% | < 3:1 | Bad — fails everything |

**Yours:**
14.3 / 21 × 100 = **68%** → Great

Quick rule of thumb: if you're above 33% (roughly one-third of max), you're in good shape. Below 21% is when text becomes genuinely hard to read.

content.text:
**What we did:**
- `colors.css` defines your dark colors (`#131313` background, `#e2e2e2` text, `#ffb3ae` accent)
- `gtk.css` imports those and adds explicit rules for window, headerbar, views, and nested lists
- `settings.ini` uses `Yaru-purple` so libadwaita loads purple accent instead of Ubuntu orange
- A fake `Yaru-purple` user theme folder blocks the system Yaru-purple CSS from loading

**Why it probably still doesn't work:**

GTK4 resolves `@define-color` variables *per provider*, not globally. Your `colors.css` runs at priority 800, but libadwaita loads its own internal color definitions separately. The user wants to try setting the `GTK_THEME` environment variable to test if GTK4 will follow a custom theme. This is a good approach - `GTK_THEME` is an environment variable that GTK4 respects and it can override the theme at a per-process level. Let me explain how to use it.

The user wants to test this before reverting to defaults. They can run:
```
GTK_THEME=Yaru-purple:dark gtk4-widget-factory
```

or just:
```
GTK_THEME=Yaru-purple gtk4-widget-factory
```
The `:dark` suffix tells GTK to prefer the dark variant. If this works, it means the theme itself is fine and the problem is with how it's being loaded through `settings.ini`.

content.text:
Yes — `GTK_THEME` overrides everything and forces a specific theme for that process. Try:

```bash
GTK_THEME=Yaru-purple:dark gtk4-widget-factory
```

The `:dark` suffix tells GTK to use the dark variant. If the purple accent and dark background appear correctly, it confirms the theme works but `settings.ini` isn't being picked up properly (or `colorreload-gtk-module` is interfering). If it still looks wrong, the issue is in the theme itself.

You can also test with just Adwaita to confirm the baseline:

```bash
GTK_THEME=Adwaita:dark gtk4-widget-factory
```
